strengths: The paper presents a coherent Algorithms/General contribution: a sparse 3D Gaussian autoencoder with lookup-free quantization, interleaved position/feature tokens, and a causal transformer with coordinate-aware 3D RoPE. The formulation is technically plausible and clearly described.

Casting Gaussian-scene synthesis as next-token prediction is an interesting alternative to the dominant diffusion/flow paradigm. A single model naturally supports unconditional sampling, prefix-based completion, and spatial extension.

The PhotoShape experiment is encouraging: the method improves FID, KID, and coverage over the reported baselines while remaining close to L3DG in MMD. The qualitative chair samples are also clean and varied.

The manuscript includes useful implementation and compute details, including voxel resolution, codebook and context sizes, losses, optimization, sampling settings, training time, and per-module optimizer parameters.

The qualitative scene results cover synthetic generation, completion, large-scale outpainting, and a preliminary ScanNet++ experiment. The appendix appropriately acknowledges reconstruction fidelity and incomplete observations as real-world limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim concerns full-scene generation, but almost all scene-level evidence is qualitative. There are no quantitative fidelity, diversity, geometry, consistency, completion, or long-horizon metrics on ASE, 3D-FRONT, or ScanNet++, making the main contribution difficult to validate objectively.

The only scene-generation baseline is L3DG, and the comparison is not well controlled: L3DG produces complete normalized scenes whereas the proposed method produces local full-scale chunks. Figure 4 therefore does not establish superiority, and relevant layout-based, autoregressive, diffusion-based, or infinite-scene methods are not experimentally compared.

The large-scene and completion claims lack quantitative stress tests. There is no measurement of boundary artifacts, degradation with outpainting distance, consistency across views, physical plausibility, conditioning fidelity, or comparison against ground truth for held-out completions.

The method is largely a combination of established components—an L3DG-style sparse Gaussian autoencoder, LFQ, GPT-style prediction, and coordinate-aware RoPE. The potentially novel integration is interesting, but the paper provides few ablations isolating its key choices: no comparison with 1D positional encoding or no RoPE, shared versus separate heads/vocabularies, LFQ versus conventional VQ, chunk/context size, or autoregression versus diffusion under the same tokenizer.

The claimed flexibility is narrower than stated. Completion operates on serialization-aligned prefixes rather than arbitrary missing regions, while large-scale generation depends on a sliding-window procedure, placement choices, and retrying empty columns up to five times. These heuristics may bias occupancy and are not ablated.

Practical scalability is weak despite the associated claims: a 12 m by 12 m scene requires about 6,000 seconds on a GH200, and disabling resampling changes runtime by roughly a factor of two. Sampling time, memory, and quality are not compared with baselines.

The PhotoShape table reports results for only 1,000 generated shapes without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or clarification that all baseline numbers use exactly matched rendering and evaluation settings. Moreover, this object-level benchmark does not compensate for the missing evaluation of the paper's primary scene-level contribution.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or model-release commitment is stated, and important details such as precise network layer configurations and the exact construction/splits of the derived 3D-FRONT Gaussian dataset are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The core idea is relevant and potentially useful: serializing vector-quantized 3D Gaussian latents for causal transformer modeling provides a unified mechanism for unconditional generation, prefix-based completion, and spatial outpainting.

The method is conceptually coherent, combining a sparse 3D autoencoder, lookup-free quantization, separate position/feature prediction heads, and coordinate-aware rotary embeddings. The presentation and system diagram make the pipeline reasonably easy to follow.

Object-level experiments on PhotoShape are promising: the method reports substantially better FID, KID, and coverage than L3DG, while obtaining comparable MMD. The qualitative chair samples are also clean and diverse.
The paper demonstrates several appealing capabilities qualitatively, including multiple completions from a common prefix, generation beyond the training extent, and transfer to ScanNet++ scenes.

Implementation details are comparatively thorough, including model sizes, context lengths, losses, compute, optimization settings, data augmentation, chunk sampling, and generation time. Prior methods and datasets are generally appropriately cited.
weaknesses: The central contribution is scene generation, but essentially all scene-level evidence is qualitative. There are no distributional, geometric, rendering-quality, diversity, completion-accuracy, physical-plausibility, or human-preference metrics on 3D-FRONT, ASE, or ScanNet++. The only substantive quantitative generative comparison concerns single-object chairs, which does not validate the main scene-level claims.

The scene comparison against L3DG is not well controlled: L3DG generates normalized full scenes, whereas the proposed model generates full-scale spatial chunks. The paper presents selected rendered images but no quantitative comparison, common spatial setting, sample statistics, or comparison with other scene-generation and completion methods. This makes superiority—or even competitiveness—on scenes impossible to establish.

Novelty is moderate. Most components are adaptations of established techniques: the Gaussian autoencoder closely follows L3DG, while LFQ, GPT-style next-token prediction, interleaved vocabularies, chunking, and coordinate-aware RoPE are existing ideas. The paper needs stronger evidence that their combination provides advantages beyond substituting an autoregressive prior for a diffusion prior.

The ablation study is very limited. It only compares serialization orders using cross-entropy, with extremely small validation differences. There are no ablations for 3D RoPE versus 1D or no positional encoding, separate prediction heads, LFQ, codebook size, chunk size/context, pretraining, resampling, or the sparse autoencoder design. Consequently, the contribution of the proposed design choices is unclear.

The autoencoder bottleneck is not evaluated independently. Reconstruction metrics and comparisons to the source Gaussian scenes are absent, even though the appendix acknowledges that reconstruction fidelity limits real-world results. Without oracle-token or reconstruction analysis, errors from compression and autoregressive modeling cannot be separated.

Completion is demonstrated only when the observed region forms a valid serialization prefix. This is materially narrower than general 3D scene completion or inpainting with arbitrary observed regions, yet the discussion sometimes suggests broader conditioning flexibility.

Long-horizon generation is supported only by selected top-down examples. There are no measurements of seam artifacts, accumulated drift, connectivity, collisions, room validity, or degradation as area increases. Moreover, empty columns are resampled up to five times, altering the learned sampling distribution and potentially concealing a significant failure mode.

The method is computationally unattractive for large environments: a 12 m by 12 m scene takes approximately 6,000 seconds on a GH200, and even a 4 m by 4 m chunk takes about 90 seconds. This weakens the scalability framing and is not compared systematically with diffusion-based inference time or quality.

The real-world study contains only qualitative completions after fine-tuning on 895 ScanNet++ scenes. Reported outputs exhibit noise and loss of detail, and there is no quantitative generalization study, held-out comparison, or unconditional real-scene evaluation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive hyperparameter reporting: the custom 3D-FRONT Gaussian preprocessing, evaluation details for rendered-view FID/KID and mesh extraction, baseline provenance, random variation, and code/model/data release plans are insufficiently specified. Overall, the interesting idea and object-level results do not compensate for the lack of rigorous evidence supporting the manuscript's primary scene-generation claims.

strengths: The paper presents an original and compelling Algorithms/General contribution: it formulates full 3D Gaussian scene synthesis as causal next-token prediction, offering a meaningful alternative to the diffusion and flow-matching paradigms dominant in this area.

The representation is technically well motivated. Sparse 3D convolutional compression, lookup-free quantization, interleaved position/feature tokens, separate prediction heads, and coordinate-aware 3D RoPE together provide a coherent route from unordered Gaussian primitives to transformer-compatible sequences.

A particularly attractive property is that one model supports unconditional generation, prefix-based completion, and spatial outpainting. The 12 m × 12 m examples and diverse completions demonstrate useful flexibility beyond fixed-size generation.

The quantitative object-level results are strong: on 1,000 PhotoShape chair samples, the method improves FID from 8.49 to 5.68, KID from 3.147 to 1.835, and coverage from 63.80 to 67.40 relative to L3DG, while retaining nearly comparable MMD (4.278 versus 4.241).

The presentation is clear and visually effective. The main pipeline is easy to follow, implementation and compute details are unusually informative, and the appendix adds real-world ScanNet++ feasibility results, sampling-speed measurements, hyperparameters, limitations, and extensive qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The main weakness is that the central scene-level claims are supported almost entirely qualitatively. There are no quantitative distribution-quality, geometry, completion, boundary-consistency, or long-horizon-coherence metrics for 3D-FRONT, ASE, or ScanNet++, even though scene generation and completion are the paper's primary focus.

The sole scene baseline comparison is limited and not fully commensurate: L3DG generates complete normalized scenes, whereas GaussianGPT generates spatial chunks. Figure 4 therefore does not establish a controlled quality advantage, and completion and large-scale outpainting have no competing baselines at all.

The ablation study is too narrow. It examines serialization order, but does not isolate the value of 3D RoPE, the fourth token-type rotary dimension, separate vocabularies and heads, lookup-free quantization, ASE pretraining, chunk placement, or empty-column resampling. The claim that 3D RoPE explains ordering insensitivity is consequently plausible but not demonstrated.

Completion is restricted to prefixes induced by the serialization order, so descriptions such as conditioning on arbitrary partial scenes or supporting general inpainting are broader than the demonstrated capability. Handling arbitrary spatial masks would require additional evidence or a modified ordering procedure.

Large-scene synthesis is computationally expensive—approximately 6,000 seconds for a 12 m × 12 m scene on a GH200—and relies on retrying empty columns up to five times. This changes the effective sampling distribution and may conceal failure rates; occupancy statistics, retry frequency, seam measurements, and comparisons of speed and quality with diffusion-based alternatives would make the practical case substantially stronger.

strengths: The paper presents an original and technically coherent Algorithms/General contribution: discrete tokenization of structured 3D Gaussians, interleaved position/feature prediction, and coordinate-aware 3D RoPE together make full-scene autoregressive generation feasible.
The unified causal formulation is practically attractive. One model supports unconditional generation, prefix-based completion, and sliding-window outpainting without task-specific architectures.

The empirical results are promising. On PhotoShape, the method substantially improves FID, KID, and coverage over L3DG; on matched 3D-FRONT chunks, it improves appearance and layout metrics and performs especially well for completion, while honestly reporting weaker unconditional geometry coverage and MMD.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering objects, synthetic scenes, real ScanNet++ data, completion, large-scene synthesis, efficiency, tokenizer design, serialization, vocabulary separation, and positional encoding. The qualitative completion samples show meaningful diversity while generally respecting context.

The appendix documents compute, optimizer settings, tokenizer trade-offs, and long-horizon degradation. Explicitly reporting the roughly 6,000-second cost of a 12 m by 12 m scene and the benefits of retry-based sampling makes the limitations easier to assess.
weaknesses: The scene-level comparison is narrow, relying almost entirely on L3DG. Comparison with additional contemporary scene-generative approaches, or a transformer baseline using the same tokenizer but a non-causal objective, would better isolate whether gains arise from autoregression rather than representation, training, or implementation differences.

Evidence for completion is limited to serialization-aligned prefixes containing the first 25% or 50% along one spatial axis. This does not substantiate broader language such as conditioning on arbitrary partial scenes, nor does it demonstrate general inpainting of holes, disjoint observations, or prefixes incompatible with the fixed xyz order.

The completion evaluation is not fully convincing. CLIP similarity between rendered completion and ground truth is a coarse measure for a multimodal task, gains over L3DG are small, and no geometric boundary-consistency, context-preservation, perceptual user study, or best-of-N-aware distributional evaluation is provided.

Large-scene synthesis remains expensive and fragile: a 12 m by 12 m scene takes about 100 minutes on a GH200, quality degrades with distance, degradation is direction-dependent because of serialization, and the reported examples rely on retrying empty columns. Thus the scalability and open-ended-generation claims should be qualified.

Real-world evidence is qualitative only and uses 895 ScanNet++ scenes after synthetic pretraining. The paper acknowledges degraded reconstruction and missing regions but provides no quantitative comparison or ablation establishing robust real-world generalization.

The ablations use cross-entropy rather than downstream rendering, geometry, completion, or outpainting metrics. The validation differences among serialization choices are also very small, so claims about the superiority or sufficiency of specific design choices are only weakly connected to perceptual performance.

Reproducibility is only partial: many hyperparameters and compute costs are given, but the manuscript does not state that code, trained models, preprocessing, or generated Gaussian datasets will be released, and exact splits, parameter counts, random seeds, variance across training runs, and uncertainty for most metrics are missing.

strengths: The paper explores a worthwhile and comparatively underdeveloped direction: autoregressive generation of full 3D Gaussian scenes. Treating occupancy and appearance as interleaved tokens offers natural prefix-conditioned completion and variable generation horizons.

The method is technically coherent: sparse Gaussian-grid compression, lookup-free quantization, separate position/feature vocabularies, and coordinate-aware 3D RoPE fit together sensibly. The ablations support the separate vocabularies and 3D positional encoding, albeit only through cross-entropy.
The PhotoShape results are strong, improving FID, KID, and coverage over the reported baselines while remaining close to L3DG in MMD.

The authors evaluate several capabilities—unconditional generation, completion, outpainting, objects, synthetic scenes, and limited real-world transfer—and candidly document inference cost and long-horizon degradation.

The appendix contains useful implementation, compute, tokenizer, reconstruction, and efficiency details. The autoencoder ablation identifies a concrete fidelity-versus-sequence-length trade-off. weaknesses: The submission does not declare a contribution type, so I assess it as Algorithms/General. Under that standard, the algorithmic novelty is modest: it largely combines an L3DG-style sparse autoencoder, LFQ, a standard causal transformer, interleaved tokens, and an adaptation of existing coordinate-aware RoPE. The main novelty is the application and formulation rather than a substantial new modeling principle.

The central scene-generation evaluation is too narrow. The only quantitative scene baseline is L3DG, and the paper omits comparisons with other recent full-scene generation approaches or autoregressive structured-3D models. This makes the broader state-of-the-art and paradigm-level claims difficult to establish.

The scene results are mixed. For unconditional generation, the proposed method is materially worse than L3DG in geometry coverage and MMD (0.548 versus 0.692 coverage and 0.118 versus 0.096 MMD). The paper frames this as a diversity trade-off, but provides no deeper analysis of mode dropping or whether improved image metrics arise from producing cleaner yet less diverse scenes.

The completion protocol covers only the first 25% or 50% along the x-axis, which aligns conveniently with the chosen serialization. It therefore does not validate arbitrary partial observations, holes, inpainting, or editing, despite language suggesting broad conditioning flexibility. CLIP similarity to a single ground-truth completion is also a weak measure for a multimodal completion task, and the small reported improvements have no uncertainty or significance analysis.

The large-scene claim rests mainly on qualitative examples and a heuristic that repeatedly rejects empty columns. Generation takes roughly 6,000 seconds for a 12 m by 12 m scene, quality deteriorates with distance, and the reported normalized tile-wise KID analysis is insufficiently defined to establish fidelity or global structural coherence. The resampling heuristic may also bias the model toward occupancy without testing physical plausibility.

Real-world evidence is only qualitative, covering a few ScanNet++ completion examples without quantitative evaluation or baselines. Thus, the experiments primarily demonstrate synthesis on curated synthetic indoor data and do not substantiate generalization to real scenes.

Several claims are overstated. The system uses an autoencoder plus a transformer rather than literally a single model, completion is not shown for arbitrary prefixes, and claims of controllable or compositional generation are not backed by semantic controls or corresponding evaluations.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix: there is no clear code/model release commitment, and important preprocessing details for constructing optimized Gaussian datasets, exact scene splits, chunk geometry, and evaluation implementation are not fully specified. Overall, the idea is promising and the object results are strong, but the limited comparative evidence and restricted scene protocols leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper presents a compelling Algorithms/General contribution: it demonstrates that next-token prediction over vector-quantized 3D Gaussian latents is a viable alternative to diffusion for full-scene generation, rather than limiting autoregressive modeling to isolated objects or meshes.

The unified formulation is elegant and practically useful. A single causal model supports unconditional synthesis, prefix-based completion, and sliding-window outpainting without task-specific architectures.

The representation and model design are technically coherent: sparse 3D compression, interleaved position/feature tokens, separate prediction heads, and coordinate-aware 3D RoPE directly address the sparsity and noncanonical ordering of 3D scenes.
Object-level results are strong. On 1,000 PhotoShape samples, the method substantially improves FID, KID, and coverage over L3DG and earlier baselines, while remaining close in MMD.

The matched 3D-FRONT experiments generally support the scene-level claims. GaussianGPT improves appearance and layout FID/KID, and its advantage becomes clearer for completion, including better MMD and CLIP similarity with 50% context.

Qualitative completions are diverse and visually consistent with the supplied context. The paper also includes useful evidence beyond headline results: serialization and positional-encoding ablations, tokenizer/reconstruction studies, inference profiling, long-horizon degradation analysis, and preliminary ScanNet++ results.

The manuscript is clear and unusually candid about important limitations, including slower sequential inference, high KV-cache memory, autoencoder fidelity, error accumulation during outpainting, and weaker unconditional geometric diversity. Training configurations and compute requirements are documented in useful detail.
weaknesses: Scene-level comparison is narrow, relying predominantly on L3DG. Broader comparisons with recent autoregressive, structured-scene, and large-world generation approaches—or a clearer explanation of why direct evaluation is impossible—would better establish the method's relative significance.

The evidence for general scene completion is more limited than some wording suggests. Quantitative tests use only serialization-compatible contiguous prefixes covering the first 25% or 50% along x; arbitrary missing regions, interior holes, and differently oriented contexts are not evaluated.

Large-scene synthesis is promising but not yet fully convincing quantitatively. Quality degrades with distance, generation of a 12 m by 12 m scene takes roughly 6,000 seconds on a GH200, and the reported examples depend on repeated empty-column resampling. More samples and comparisons against alternative outpainting systems would strengthen this claim.

The scene metrics provide incomplete evidence of semantic and physical plausibility. Gaussian-center Chamfer statistics, rendering FID/KID, and CLIP similarity may not expose collisions, floating objects, navigability failures, or violations of the observed completion boundary; semantic or human evaluation would be valuable.

Unconditional scene generation exhibits a meaningful geometry-diversity trade-off: compared with L3DG, coverage falls from 0.692 to 0.548 and MMD worsens from 0.096 to 0.118, despite improved appearance and layout metrics. Thus, claims of broadly superior scene generation should remain qualified.

Real-world validation is qualitative and limited to fine-tuning on 895 ScanNet++ scenes. The shown results support feasibility, but do not yet demonstrate robust real-world generation or quantify the effect of missing observations and non-axis-aligned geometry.

Autoregressive inference is substantially slower and more memory-intensive than L3DG for unconditional generation: 78.1 seconds and 5.04 GB versus 23.8 seconds and 1.55 GB per chunk. This weakens any implied general efficiency advantage, though the paper reports the limitation transparently.

Several components are adaptations of established techniques—L3DG-style compression, lookup-free quantization, GPT modeling, and multidimensional RoPE—so the originality lies primarily in their effective integration and validation for Gaussian scene generation rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.
